schools.summary: Henry reads the enemies' scorn as first a matter of the heart — indignation that a walled Jerusalem would be fenced against them — then of word, the ridicule that ironically kept them idle till too late.
Ellicott notes the writer's method: a general statement of mockery is made here and expanded in the following verses.
Gill fixes the tense — 'were building,' the wall not yet finished — so the enemy rages at a work barely begun.
Clarke frames the whole chapter's campaign and the enemies' method of discrediting God's work by first despising the workmen.

themes: news of the rebuilding reaches Samaria
the strength of the church vexes its foes
contempt that leaves the work unhindered

schools.summary: Keil parses the taunt as four present-tense questions before the rulers and army of Samaria, notes the rare word 'feeble,' and rejects the 'leave them alone' gloss; Ellicott names the hearers as counsellors and body-guard and ties 'will they sacrifice?' to the provocation of v.5.

Clarke reads the verse as a catalogue of the enemies' tactics — despising, ridicule, lying, deceit (cf. Neh. 6:2); Wesley catches the mockery of the timescale ('in a day') and of the burnt, shattered stones.
Gill names Tobiah, Geshem, and other governors as the audience Sanballat harangued.

themes: mockery before the army of Samaria
the burnt stones of the ruins

schools.summary: Henry reads Tobiah's jest about the fox as scorn of the work itself (as Sanballat scorned the workmen), and finds in the pairing the law that 'profane scoffers sharpen one another' and that unlikely allies unite in mocking good work.
Gill fixes Tobiah the Ammonite at Sanballat's side, one of the brethren before whom the mockery was publicly made.

Henry commends Nehemiah's appeal that God notice the slights on his despised people, but marks the turning-back of the reproach as a spirit of prophecy, not a pattern for Christians taught by Christ to pray 'Father, forgive them' (Luke 23:34).

Keil traces the committal of the whole matter to God — turn the reproach on their head, give them for plunder in captivity; Ellicott describes Nehemiah's habit of turning all to devotion and the OT tone of holy revenge.

Clarke judges such a prayer, taken literally, not lawful for a Christian bound by Matt. 5:44, excusable only in a Jew under irritation; Wesley glosses the plea to give the enemies for a prey and captivity.
Gill notes Nehemiah sent the scoffers no answer but applied wholly to God.
Gill reads the imprecation not as private revenge but a public zeal for God's glory, indeed a prophecy of certain judgment (like David's psalms), grounded in God's threat against Ammon and Moab.

Clarke takes the terrible words as declaratory ('their sin shall not be blotted out'), touching only bodies and lives — what a man sows he reaps (Gal. 6:7); Wesley reads a plea that judgment fall so the enemies be reformed or others warned.
Keil glosses 'not blotted out' as 'not left unpunished,' the ground being that the enemies provoked God's wrath before the builders.
Henry, judging the enemies' hearts hardened, roots the anger in offence to God ('they have provoked thee,' Ps. 74:22), yet holds the imprecation not to be imitated.

debates.question: How is Nehemiah's imprecation against the enemies to be understood, and may a Christian pray it?

sides.position: A righteous, prophetic declaration of just judgment for the honour of God — not personal vindictiveness — touching only the enemies' bodies and lives
An utterance belonging to the old dispensation, spoken by a spirit of prophecy, not a pattern for Christians who are taught by Christ to bless and pray for their enemies

schools.summary: Henry reads the wall's swift rise to half-height as the fruit of a willing heart — 'good work goes on well when people have a mind to it' — and turns the enemies' reproach into a spur, not a deterrent.

Keil explains the wall was joined throughout its circumference to half its height with no gap left, ascribing the speed to 'the people had a heart to work'; Ellicott confirms it was continuous up to half its height.
Clarke presses the emphatic 'a heart to work' — where the heart is engaged God's work prospers — and notes the whole verse is omitted by the Septuagint.
Gill: they built on notwithstanding the scoffs and threats.

themes: the wall joined to half its height
reproach as a spur to duty
God's work prospers with willing hands

schools.summary: Henry anatomizes the enemies' wrath — envy of the Jews' piety and prosperity — and marks the plot as unanimous, secret, and cruel, latent already in this kindling of anger.

Keil and Ellicott read the occasion — the walls 'made up' and breaches stopped, the wall now continuous — with Ellicott noting the confederate tribes were only small parties under Sanballat's influence.
Gill enumerates the widened alliance: Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians under Geshem, Ammonites, and Ashdodites.

Henry reads the combination as unanimous (rival interests united against God's work), secret ('digged deep to hide it from the Lord'), and cruel ('we will come and slay them'), yet doomed — good work is God's work and shall prosper.
Ellicott notes the plot's boldness against Persian authority (soon abandoned) and reads 'to hinder it' rather as 'to do it hurt.'
Gill states the fact: all the named peoples entered a confederacy and combination.

themes: a plot of surprise and slaughter
good work God will not let cease

schools.summary: Henry makes the verse the rule 'watch and pray' (Matt. 26:41): prayer first and always, then the watch — prayer without watchfulness tempts God, watchfulness without prayer slights him.

Clarke teaches that confidence in God does not preclude the means of defence — God works in us to will and to do (Phil. 2:12-13), yet we must use the power he gives, for power and its use are distinct.
Ellicott reads 'because of them' as 'over against them,' the watch set opposite each point of the enemy's camp, joined to solemn united prayer.
Gill reads the prayer as spreading the whole case before God for direction and help.

themes: confidence and the use of means

schools.summary: Henry sets the builders' 'let it fall' against the enemies' 'let us cause the work to cease,' marvels that valiant Judah should faint, and notes leaders wrestle as much with friends' fears as with foes' terrors.

Keil traces the decay of strength to the day-and-night watch added to labour and the much rubbish; Ellicott treats the verse as a summary of the growing feebleness as hands were diverted to the watches.
Clarke pictures the exhausting day-and-night toil of clearing ruins before founding a new wall; Wesley reads the Jews terrified and wearied, minded to desist for a season.
Gill attributes the complaint to several of the men of Judah.

themes: the strength of the bearers decayed

schools.summary: Keil ties the enemies' boast ('they shall not know... till we slay them') to the deepening of the Jews' discouragement; Ellicott fixes the strategy as a plan to watch and surprise rather than openly attack.
Henry answers the confident plot with his refrain: bad men aim to hinder good work, but good work is God's work and shall prosper.
Gill glosses 'they shall not know' — the enemies' designs concealed.

themes: a plot of ambush and surprise

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott read the repeated message as a summons: the outlying Jews, ringed by enemies on all four sides, urged their brethren 'from all places, return to us' for common protection.

Wesley reads a warning of invasion 'every way,' the 'ten times' a round number; Clarke calls the verse extremely difficult, prefers the LXX ('they come up against us'), and floats an emendation ('what they designed') though no MS supports it.
Henry reads the intelligence for its providence — God brings the enemies' devices to light, making even lukewarm neighbours his spies, so that 'a bird of the air shall carry their voice.'
Gill sets the scene: Jews near Samaria, Arabia, and Ashdod bring intelligence of the enemies' designs.

debates.question: What does the neighbouring Jews' obscure, repeated message mean?

sides.position: A summons calling the scattered builders home 'to us' for mutual protection, since enemies pressed from every side
A warning that the enemies would come up against them from every quarter ('they will be upon you every way')
The received text is corrupt; read 'what the enemies designed against us' (an emendation with no manuscript support), following the LXX's 'they come up from all places against us'

themes: intelligence from Jews among the enemies

schools.summary: Keil calls the verse hardly intelligible, reading 'lowest' and 'bare' places whence foes might be seen; Ellicott identifies the 'lower' with the 'bare' places and the not-yet-raised sections, families set besides the appointed guards.

Henry reads the tactics — guards behind the low wall as a breastwork, upon the high wall to cast down stones — and the wisdom of setting families together so mutual relation engages mutual assistance.
Wesley takes 'behind' as within the unfinished lower walls, and 'higher' as the finished tops and towers whence to shoot arrows and throw stones.
Gill sets the guards where the wall was lowest and most easily breached or scaled.

themes: an obscure disposition of the guard

schools.summary: Henry builds the encouragement on whom they fight under (the Lord great and terrible, before whom enemies are mean — the fear of God the antidote to the fear of man, Isa. 51:12-13) and whom they fight for (brethren, sons, daughters, Ps. 122:8).
Keil gives the full charge — 'be not afraid... the Lord will fight for you' (Deut. 20:3) — and Ellicott sets the appeal at the actual approach of an attacking party.
Clarke turns it to a challenge (are the enemies stronger than God?) and a call to fight for altars and hearths (with the parallel from Aeschylus); Wesley reads 'looked' as looking up to God.
Gill reads 'I looked' as surveying the armed and posted people.

debates.question: What did Nehemiah 'look' at when he rose to encourage the people?

sides.position: He looked up to God, committing himself and his cause to divine protection
He surveyed his own people, seeing them posted and armed
He saw the enemy's actual approach, and the appeal was uttered as the attackers drew near

themes: the fear of God against the fear of man

schools.summary: Keil reads the design circumvented and the Jews returned to a guarded labour (half working, half armed); Ellicott admires how the verse condenses the frustration and the standing-down of the special guard.
Henry unfolds the happy disappointment — a plot of surprise quashed once known — and the builders' cheerful return, God's care of our safety a spur to renewed duty.
Clarke notes the word 'counsel' brought to nought countenances his proposed emendation at the earlier difficult verse.
Gill: the enemies heard their design was known from the Jews' preparations to defend themselves.

themes: return to the work with cheer
God's care a spur to duty

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott set out the division — half of Nehemiah's own servants (his retinue, distinct from the house of Judah) build while half bear spears, shields, bows, and habergeons (coats of mail), the rulers posted behind to lead the defence.

Clarke likens it to armed guards over Palestinian sowers and glosses the habergeon as a breastplate; Wesley reads the measure as a renewed precaution, the rulers behind to encourage, assist, and command.
Henry draws the spiritual pattern — arms never laid down, half working and half guarding by turns to ease the weary — finding in it the Christian who is at once builder and soldier all his days.
Gill dates the arrangement from the alarm of danger.

themes: weapons at hand for the labourers
the rulers behind the house of Judah

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the verse fairly literally: the burden-bearers held a weapon in one hand while carrying with the other, the masons built with both hands and kept their weapons at their side.
Clarke (with Ovid) and Wesley take 'one hand' as proverbial for arms kept ready — Wesley turning it to working out salvation with the weapons of our warfare in hand.
Henry holds the phrase cannot be literal (the work needs both hands) but means the builders were equally employed in labour and defence — every Christian a labourer and a soldier at once.

debates.question: Is 'every one with one hand wrought, and with the other held a weapon' to be taken literally?

sides.position: Partly literal — the burden-bearers really carried a weapon in one hand, while the masons built two-handed with weapons at their side
Figurative and proverbial — a picture of armed readiness, since building needs both hands; the arms were kept ready at hand

themes: working with one hand, armed with the other
the Christian as labourer and soldier

schools.summary: Henry reads the girded sword as the emblem of Scripture, 'the sword of the Spirit' (Eph. 6:17), carried always at hand, and the ever-ready trumpeter as Nehemiah's provision for early alarm.
Gill notes each builder wrought with his sword girded on, prepared in a moment for either service.
Wesley fixes the trumpet's office — to call the people together whenever and wherever needed.

themes: the sword girded at the side
the word of God as the sword of the Spirit
early alarm for a scattered work

schools.summary: Keil gives the charge — the work great and wide, the builders separated far apart; at the trumpet's sound all are to assemble, for 'our God will fight for us' — the danger lying in the dispersion of the workforce.

Henry shows how Nehemiah met the peril of a scattered work — continually walking the rounds to oversee and to give speedy notice by the trumpet — and grounds the whole in the promise that God will fight for them.
Gill marks the charge given alike to nobles, rulers, and all the people at the building.
Keil pairs the summons ('resort thither unto us') with its ground ('our God shall fight for us'); Gill notes the order reached every worker, even the most distant.
Clarke explains the tactic — an extensive wall and scattered workmen, kept as near together as possible, with a trumpeter always by Nehemiah to gather all to the point of danger.
Henry marks the passage from dispersed labour to close-order defence at the alarm, all done in assurance that God would fight — as Christ's labourers should unite against a common foe.

themes: dispersed to build, gathered to fight

schools.summary: Henry reads the spears held up (their very sight terrifying the enemy) from twilight to twilight as the pattern of the believer's unremitting watch against the rulers of darkness (Eph. 6:12).
Ellicott takes the verse as a recapitulation with its note of the day's length — labour from the rising of the morning till the stars appeared.
Gill notes the standing division — the work carried on while half held the spears.

themes: from dawn till the stars appeared
a watch that outlasts the daylight

schools.summary: Keil gives the order — every man with his servant to lodge within Jerusalem, a guard by night and labourers by day — the abstract terms standing for the watchers and workers themselves.
Clarke explains the change of habit — country people kept from returning home, obliged to sleep in the city to be ready for a night attack — judging all Nehemiah's arrangements wise and judicious.
Henry gathers the maxim that a city's strength lies more in its hands than its walls — secure the men and God's blessing on them, and be secure.

themes: a guard by night, labour by day
concentrating the force behind the gates
a city's strength in its men

schools.summary: Keil confesses the closing 'every one his weapon water' very obscure and unyielding, inviting emendation; Ellicott, rejecting our version and the 'weapon was his water' turn, supplies the ellipsis 'every man went with his weapon to the water.'

Clarke canvasses the versions (Vulgate, LXX, Syriac) and prefers De Rossi's manuscript reading — garments laid aside only to be sent to washing; Wesley reads the plain sense of cleansing from impurity.
Henry sets aside the philology to praise the devotion — men who slept in their clothes because their heart was on the work, 'good work goes on well when those who labour make a business of it.'
Gill marks the company — Nehemiah, his brethren, servants, and guard — who put off their clothes for none of it.

debates.question: How is the obscure closing clause ('every one his weapon water') to be rendered?

sides.position: The garments were put off only for washing — clothes sent to be washed, or cleansing from impurity
Each man kept his weapon with him even when he went to the water: 'every man went with his weapon to the water'
The text is corrupt and yields no tolerable sense as it stands, requiring emendation
